item.title: Israel election masks economic fault lines as war spending surges
item.description: Soaring defence spending, rising debt, talent outflows and ultra-Orthodox exemptions pose long-term economic challenges despite strong headline growth ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Galit Altstein Israel’s election campaign has been consumed by Iran, national security and the impact of three years of war, with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, rarely straying from the theme. Those fixations belie a sobering reality for Israeli households: overshadowing Tuesday’s ballot is is an economic schism that the next government will have to address. The vote will pit Netanyahu’s military hawkishness and religious nationalism against Eisenkot’s plans to fund Israel’s defense buildup through structural reforms that help bring down the government’s debt, which has soared in the past three years. Eisenkot, a retired general, wants to prioritize integrating the rapidly growing ultra-orthodox population, which is largely exempt from military service and heavily subsidized by the government, into the defense forces and the labor market. In Netanyahu’s vision, Israel should become a “Super Sparta” and spend hundreds of billions of shekels to achieve greater military self-reliance. “For years, we kept defense spending under control to encourage economic growth,” he said on Friday. “Now the economy must support defense, because without security, there will be no economy.” He drew criticism, including from the central bank, by saying — in a nod to Israel’s growing isolation — that it should prepare to circumvent possible international sanctions by using cryptocurrencies as part of “an alternative economic system.” “The upcoming elections represent a crossroads for the economy, with the outcome likely to have significant implications,” said Rafael Gozlan, chief economist at the Tel Aviv-based IBI Investment House. More than a guns-versus-butter debate, the divide is over how far Israel will go to pay for its guns. On the surface, Israel’s economy is thriving against the backdrop of war. Foreign direct investment hit a record $26 billion last year, while growth — fueled by the tech industry — is expected to outperform peers this year and the shekel is among the world’s top-performing currencies. Economists, however, warn the incoming government will inherit severe structural vulnerabilities. Whoever the next leader is, they must navigate a skyrocketing defense budget, the international isolation, a brain drain and demographic imbalances that threaten to paralyze the economy long after the ballots are counted. The cost of living, a long-running source of social unease, especially when it comes to housing, remains one of the highest in the OECD, alongside Iceland and Switzerland. “Resilience is not equivalent to prosperity,” a group of researchers from the Tel-Aviv-based Institute for National Security Studies said in a report this month. Israel is channeling a bigger portion of its national resources to defense, “unavoidably at the expense of long-term investment in growth engines and in civilian services.” Gross domestic product per capita has barely changed since Hamas’s attack in October 2023 triggered the start of multiple wars. On Wednesday, the central bank raised its growth projections to 5.6% for this year and 7.5% for 2027. Still, Governor Amir Yaron said that “rapid growth may create a distorted picture of the pace of real domestic economic activity.” The numbers are heightened by the so-called “Nvidia effect,” he said. That refers to the huge revenues earned by the US chip designer’s Israeli arm, which help boost tax revenue but do little to support local investment and jobs. Excluding Nvidia, the economy would grow just 3.4% this year. The mobilization of tens of thousands of Israelis during the war, keeping them away from their businesses, is one of the headwinds awaiting the next government. That will complicate keeping the budget deficit under control. Paying for Guns While ceasefires have reduced the intensity of the various conflicts, Israel’s forces are still occupying parts of Gaza, Lebanon and Syria. They’re conducting daily operations in the West Bank, pushing up expenditure on salaries and munitions. The war with Iran, meanwhile, may be about to escalate. The opposition largely accepts Israel’s new preemptive military approach, so it’s likely the defense bill will remain elevated regardless of the voting on Tuesday. Israel’s defense budget stands at almost 8% of GDP this year — the highest share among its Western peers — and Netanyahu has proposed a 450-billion-shekel ($145 billion) buildup over 12 years. If the plan goes ahead, the central bank sees debt increasing to as high as 85% of output through 2035. While still fairly low by today’s rich-world standards, it was only around 60% before Hamas’s attack. Retaining Talent While Netanyahu’s government boasts of Israel’s military and economic achievements, the opposition argues that finances are stretched and the country risks a mass departure of the country’s most productive citizens. “When I ask audiences at parlor meetings what their greatest fear is if Netanyahu stays in power, the most common answer is: ‘That my kids pack up and leave the country,’” said Shaul Meridor, a former Finance Ministry official now running with Eisenkot.Some 100,000 Israelis left the country in 2023 and 2024, far more than in previous years, according to a Tel Aviv University study. Academics, engineers, physicians and other high-earners featured prominently among them and preliminary data suggest the trend continued into 2025. The exodus began to take shape after Netanyahu’s government embarked on a push to curb judicial powers and continued through the war, as many Israelis sought respite from repeated missile attacks and relentless reserve duty. Finance Ministry Chief Economist Shmuel Abramzon said emigration hasn’t reached macroeconomic-relevant levels, but acknowledges the trend is concerning.  Ultra-Orthodox Exemptions Netanyahu has resisted drafting ultra-Orthodox men into military service, in defiance of a Supreme Court ruling fiercely opposed by religious parties that have long been kingmakers in his coalitions. That’s meant tens of thousands of reservists were called to serve, including some of the nation’s most skilled tech workers. The opposition and economists argue this can be resolved by drafting thousands of eligible ultra-Orthodox men to the military. Authorities say mobilizing civilians who have already done mandatory service is far more expensive than integrating Israelis yet to do so. An opposition-led government would be more likely to pursue those goals while “potentially winding down some active military fronts,” said Gozlan of IBI Investment House. The current coalition, he believes, “would be reluctant to end existing military campaigns and has failed to pursue a more equitable distribution of the military service burden.” The challenge has loomed for years, but the war has pushed it to the forefront of politics. Many secular and observant Jews alike resent seeing loved ones risk their lives in combat, leaving families, businesses and studies for months while others remain exempt. The economic implications of Israel’s growing religious population extend well beyond the military. One in four first-graders attends an independent ultra-Orthodox school, where core subjects like math and English are often neglected. That risks leaving the country with an increasing share of the workforce sidelined from high-income jobs and overly reliant on subsidies. “We must integrate the Ultra-Orthodox and Arab communities,” Meridor said. “It starts by terminating all budgets for schools who don’t teach a core curriculum.”  The Bank of Israel has voiced similar concerns. It’s also called for measures to address a chronic under-investment in public services, which in 2025 lagged the OECD’s 43% share of economic output by ten percentage points. That’s translated into long wait times to see medical specialists and record-low scores by Israeli students in the PISA comparative assessment.

item.title: Brazil votes in tight presidential runoff between Lula and Bolsonaro
item.description: Brazil's presidential runoff pits Lula against Flavio Bolsonaro, with voters weighing economic concerns, crime and US relations amid a closely contested election ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Brazil votes in tight presidential runoff between Lula and Bolsonaro

Brazil votes in tight presidential runoff between Lula and Bolsonaro Brazil's presidential runoff pits Lula against Flavio Bolsonaro, with voters weighing economic concerns, crime and US relations amid a closely contested election

A person stands at a voting booth during the Brazilian presidential runoff election, in Porto Alegre, Brazil October 25, 2026. REUTERS/Diego Vara

Reuters 4 min read Last Updated : Oct 25 2026 | 10:57 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Brazilians voted on Sunday in a tight runoff that could move Latin America's largest nation sharply rightward, bringing it closer to the United States as part of a broader conservative shift across the region.   The runoff pits leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva against right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro. Flavio scored a major upset at the start of the month by defying pollsters to lead the voting in the first round.   A victory for Bolsonaro, 45, would extend a wave of right-wing victories for Latin American candidates friendly to US President Donald Trump, while a fourth mandate for Lula would be a disappointment in Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security.

Washington denies accusations of meddling   Reuters on Saturday revealed a campaign within Trump's State Department to help get the Bolsonaros back into power. Also Read

Trump confuses Brazil with India on prez election, says 125 million voted

Trump has so far declined to endorse a candidate. Asked on Sunday who he hoped would win, Trump declined to say.   "I don't want to get into that, but we are watching," he told reporters in Washington.   Brazil's election race has been dominated by corruption scandals, economic anxiety and accusations of US meddling, which Washington denies. It has also been coloured by the fallout from Jair Bolsonaro's 2025 conviction for plotting a 2022 coup, with Flavio pledging to free his father if elected.

Trump has called the case a "witch hunt" and imposed a 50 per cent tariff on Brazil in 2025, in a decision explicitly linked to Jair Bolsonaro's trial. While this was later watered down, Trump unleashed new levies against Brazil this year, citing unfair trade practices.   Lula has cast the Trump administration's proximity to the Bolsonaro clan as part of an attempt to sway the election, while labelling tariffs and other punitive measures as bullying.   "We can't just hand Brazil over," said Elenildes dos Reis, a 60-year-old lawyer in Sao Paulo who voted for Lula and said his victory would be a way of standing up to Trump and what she described as a rising wave of fascism.

"It won't just be our victory, it will be the world's," she said.   On economic issues, despite falling inequality and unemployment, Lula has struggled to win over an electorate grappling with high living costs and heavy household debt.   Endemic gang violence also weighs on voters' minds.   Bolsonaro has sought to capitalise on cost-of-living concerns and has promised a heavy-handed approach to fighting crime, pledging maximum-security jails and chemical castration for serious sexual offences.   "We need change," said Jose Carlos Jarra, a 61-year-old retiree in Sao Paulo who worked in healthcare and voted for Bolsonaro. He hoped the senator would tackle public security and do more for retirees, calling Brazil's minimum wage "a disgrace".

In Rio de Janeiro, 75-year-old retiree Alba Marques said her vote for Bolsonaro was a vote against Lula's Workers' Party, not for Bolsonaro.   "I can't stand 40 years of a guy saying he's going to fix Brazil anymore. The same promise," she said.   Candidates are neck and neck   Casting his ballot in Rio de Janeiro on Sunday, Bolsonaro urged people to come out to vote "come rain or shine". Lula voted in Sao Bernardo do Campo, near Sao Paulo, and thanked his supporters. "What the people did for me these past few days is something I can never repay," he told reporters.   Polls show the candidates practically tied going into the runoff.

Historical precedent favours Bolsonaro, however, as no candidate has ever won the presidency after coming second in the first-round vote.   Bolsonaro picked up 47 per cent of ballots cast in the first round, while Lula trailed with 45 per cent.   The senator's first-round win sent Brazil's markets and currency soaring on expectations of pro-business reforms.   His first-round success was mirrored in congressional elections for his Liberal Party and other right-wing politicians, which could pave a legislative path for him or complicate governance for Lula.

Home / Markets / News / Q2 results, US Fed decision, crude oil may drive stock markets this week

Q2 results, US Fed decision, crude oil may drive stock markets this week Besides, Jio Platforms' market debut, trading activity of foreign investors and global trends would also dictate investors' sentiment

In a holiday-shortened last week, the 30-share BSE Sensex tumbled 1,605.44 points, or 2.15 per cent, while the 50-share NSE Nifty slumped 546.15 points, or 2.36 per cent | Image: Bloomberg

Press Trust of India New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 25 2026 | 10:36 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Quarterly earnings, the US Fed interest rate decision, movement in crude oil and developments related to West Asia tensions will be the key divers for stock markets this week, analysts said.   Besides, Jio Platforms' market debut, trading activity of foreign investors and global trends would also dictate investors' sentiment, they added.   "Investors will track September industrial production and manufacturing output data on October 28. Corporate earnings will remain a key driver, with TVS Motor, Asian Paints, Trent, Sun Pharma, Bharat Electronics, Indian Oil, Bank of Baroda and GAIL India, among others, scheduled to announce their results," Ajit Mishra, SVP - Research, Religare Broking, said.

The US Federal Reserve's interest rate decision on Wednesday, October 28, will be the key global event, he said, adding that investors will closely examine the policy statement and accompanying commentary for signals on the future interest rate trajectory.   "Movements in US Treasury yields, crude oil prices, geopolitical developments and broader global risk appetite will also influence domestic market direction," Mishra added. Also Read

Stock Market Close: Sensex falls for 4th day, ends 126 pts lower; Nifty at 22,600; VIX rises 6%

"The US Federal Reserve's October 27-28 meeting will be the principal global trigger. Markets largely expect rates to remain unchanged, making the policy guidance more important than the decision itself. A continued focus on inflation could push US yields and the dollar higher and keep foreign flows into emerging markets under pressure, while balanced guidance may support a temporary recovery in global equities," Hariselvan Radhakrishnan, Founder & CEO of HST Wealth, a Research Analyst firm, said.

Domestically, industrial production data and quarterly earnings will determine whether India's resilient growth outlook can counter the external pressure, he said.   Meanwhile, Jio Platforms shares are scheduled to debut on the stock exchanges on October 28 and will be a key sentiment trigger for the primary market.   "Crude oil remains a central concern. Prices at elevated levels amid escalating geopolitical tensions threaten to push up India's energy import bill, complicate the inflation outlook and add pressure on the rupee and corporate margins.    The US Federal Reserve's upcoming monetary policy meeting will be another key event for global markets. Investors will look for signals on the interest rate outlook, particularly as elevated US Treasury yields continue to influence the dollar and global risk appetite," Ponmudi R, CEO - Enrich Money, an online trading and wealth tech firm, said.

In a holiday-shortened last week, the 30-share BSE Sensex tumbled 1,605.44 points, or 2.15 per cent, while the 50-share NSE Nifty slumped 546.15 points, or 2.36 per cent.
